newsitem.title: USA: Rat-borne tropical disease in U.S. inner cities.
newsitem.headline: Rat-borne tropical disease in U.S. inner cities.

text.p: Deteriorating U.S. inner cities may provide a previously unrecognized breeding ground for a rat-borne disease that can be fatal to humans, a medical journal reported Thursday.

The disease, leptospirosis, was diagnosed between 1993 and 1995 in three inner-city Baltimore residents who reported being exposed to rats, acccording to the report in the current issue of Annals of Internal Medicine.

All three recovered after treatment, but their infections illustrated that social and economic decay in inner cities could lead to the spread of diseases previously unknown in such areas, said the report, written by researchers at Johns Hopkins University and the National Institutes of Health.

"Our results suggest that leptospirosis may be yet another re-emerging infectious disease in urban areas of the United States," it said. "Leptospirosis may become increasingly recognised in deteriorating inner cities in which rat populations are expanding."

Leptospirosis is a bacterial illness that usually occurs in tropical climates and is most commonly spread to humans through contact with the urine of infected animals. It can cause flulike symptoms, jaundice, kidney failure and sometimes death.
In the United States, where the disease is rare, most cases come from contact with farm livestock, dogs and rats, the report said.
In the Baltimore cases, two of the patients reported cutting themselves on glass in rat-infested alleys, and the third reported walking barefoot in harbour areas where rats had been seen.
The study said indications of the leptospirosis bacterium had been found in 19 of 21 rats trapped in the alleys where it was believed the patients had been infected.
